The Story of King Padmarath

I bow to the feet of Lord Jina, worshipped by Indra, Dharanendra, the Vidyadhars, kings, and maharajas, and I write the story of King Padmarath, who was a renowned devotee of the Jinas.

In the land of Magadh stood a beautiful city named Mithila. Its king was Padmarath — wise, skilled in statecraft, generous, and benevolent. He was widely celebrated for his virtues.

One day Padmarath went hunting in the forest. He spotted a hare and galloped after it on his horse. The hare vanished from sight, and by fortune the king arrived at a cave called Kalgufa. There lived an ascetic named Sudharm, a great penancer whose divine body radiated extraordinary brilliance through the power of his austerities. Padmarath, seeing this supremely peaceful monk adorned with the three jewels of right faith, knowledge, and conduct, felt his own agitation subside — as red-hot iron is calmed by water. He dismounted at once, bowed to the sage with devotion, and listened to his sacred teachings on dharma. The discourse pleased him greatly, and he accepted the lesser vows with right faith.

Afterwards, Padmarath asked the sage, "O Lord! O support of the world! Tell me, is there any other moon-like being who increases the ocean of Jain dharma as you do? If so, where is he? O ocean of compassion, dispel my doubt."

The sage replied, "O King! At this time, in the city of Champa, the twelfth Tirthankara, Lord Vasupujya, is present. The brilliance of his physical body cannot be matched by many suns together, and between my finite knowledge and his infinite qualities there is the difference between a mustard seed and Mount Meru." Hearing of Lord Vasupujya, Padmarath was filled with an intense longing to behold him. He set out at once with great splendour to see the Lord.

Two deities named Dhanvantari and Vishvanulom learned of this and descended to the middle world to test Padmarath. To examine the firmness of his devotion, they subjected him to many trials on the road — a fearsome black serpent, the breaking of his royal umbrella, fire breaking out, fierce winds hurling rocks and mountains, untimely torrential rain, and many other terrifying calamities. Yet Padmarath remained unmoved. His faith did not waver, for he had taken refuge in the Lord and trusted that whatever happened was the fruit of his own karma.

Pleased by his steadfastness, the deities revealed themselves and blessed him. Padmarath reached Lord Vasupujya and beheld the radiant form of the Tirthankara. Overcome with devotion, he prostrated before the Lord and received his teaching. He spent his remaining days in pious service, deepening his faith and practising dharma with unwavering devotion.

This story teaches that true devotion, once firmly rooted, cannot be shaken by any worldly trial. Those who take refuge in the Lord with sincere faith shall overcome every obstacle and attain the supreme goal.
